text: Chapter 1 was honest up front that CMDB data quality is genuinely hard, and that it decays by default unless something actively measures it. That's not the same as saying it's unmeasurable, though. This lesson shows the real, built-in tool ServiceNow gives you to measure that decay instead of guessing at it: the CMDB Health Dashboard, built on the Service Mapping and CMDB Health application.

The dashboard scores four separate dimensions, each defined per CI class. Completeness asks whether the fields that actually matter are populated on each CI -- a server record with a blank Operational Status and no assigned Support Group is structurally present but practically useless. Correctness asks whether the populated data actually passes validation and makes logical sense, catching things like a CPU count of zero or an install date sitting in the future. Compliance checks alignment with the Identification and Reconciliation rules the next lesson covers. And duplicate rate tracks what percentage of CIs in a class are likely duplicating another record already sitting in the table.

Before a dashboard like this exists, 'is our CMDB any good' gets answered by anecdote -- an auditor spot-checks twenty records, finds a few obviously stale ones, and the answer becomes whatever story gets told afterward in a meeting. The dashboard replaces that anecdote with a defensible, repeatable score you can trend week over week or quarter over quarter, with a drill-down to exactly which fields on exactly which records are the problem.

A score only matters once someone acts on it. A Completeness score of seventy-one percent on server CIs, up from sixty-four percent last quarter, points straight at a bounded task -- populate Operational Status on the three hundred and forty specific records still missing it, not a vague instruction to 'fix the CMDB.' A low duplicate-rate score points toward the detection and merge work two lessons from now, and a low Compliance score points at a specific rule that needs tightening.

Four dimensions, each scored and trended, turning a subjective impression into a concrete, actionable backlog -- and a way to tell, over time, whether a governance effort is actually working or just moved the problem around. Next up: the Identification and Reconciliation rules that actually drive two of those four scores -- what makes a CI unique, and which source wins when two systems disagree about it.
